name: Audit Mindset Basics

quiz.text: What is an 'audit mindset' in the context of security?

answers.text: A financial accounting technique for tracking expenses.
A habit of questioning and verifying requests before acting, especially unusual or urgent ones.
A government-required security certification.
A software tool for detecting malware.

quiz.text: Which of the following are red flags that should trigger verification? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Requests that bypass normal approval procedures.
Extreme urgency with pressure to act immediately.
The requester being conveniently unavailable for discussion.
Requests that follow standard company procedures.
Requests involving unfamiliar vendors or recipients.

quiz.text: You receive an urgent email from your CEO asking you to purchase gift cards immediately. What is the best first step?

answers.text: Purchase the gift cards quickly to help the CEO.
Reply to the email asking for more details.
Call the CEO using a phone number from your contacts (not from the email) to verify the request.
Forward the email to a colleague to get their opinion.

quiz.text: Why is it important to verify requests through a different communication channel?

answers.text: It creates a paper trail for accounting purposes.
The attacker controls the channel the request arrived on (a lookalike domain or a hacked mailbox), but not the phone number you already hold.
Company policy requires all requests to be made twice.
It makes the verification process more formal.

quiz.text: What is a Business Email Compromise (BEC) attack?

answers.text: A virus that spreads through email attachments.
An attack where criminals impersonate trusted parties (like executives) to trick employees into transferring money or data.
A type of spam filter bypass technique.
Software that automatically responds to business emails.

quiz.text: Which of the following are good practices when you suspect a fraudulent request? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Report the incident to IT Security, even if you're not 100% certain it's malicious.
Process part of the request while waiting for verification.
Document the red flags you identified and the steps you took to verify.
Never ask for verification because it might offend the requester.
Use contact information from your existing records, not information provided in the suspicious message.

steps.name: Nine Dollars
steps.description: He is not going to break into anything. He is going to buy a domain that reads like the real one at a glance.
steps.instructions: Register the lookalike domain.

steps.name: One Character

highlighterTexts: meridiananalytics.co against the real meridiananalytics.com. One character, at the end, where nobody looks.
Catch-all mail, live in under four minutes. He now sends genuinely authenticated mail from a domain he genuinely owns, so every technical check the recipient runs will pass.
Nothing at Meridian has been touched. There is no compromise to detect, which is why the only defence left is a person deciding to check.

steps.description: That is the entire technical component of this attack.
steps.instructions: Review what nine dollars bought.

steps.name: An Urgent Request

email.message:
Hi Alice,

I need you to process an urgent payment to one of our vendors. They've threatened to halt services if we don't pay by end of day.

Please transfer $47,500 to:
Vendor: TechStream Solutions
Account: 7829104563
Routing: 021000089
Bank: First National Bank

I'm in back-to-back meetings so I can't discuss this now. Please process immediately and confirm when done.

Thanks,
David
email.subject: Urgent: Vendor Payment - Need Today

steps.description: Thursday afternoon. A payment request arrives from David Chen, the CFO. Your first instinct is to help - he is your manager, the request is plausible, and you do not want to be the reason a vendor walks. That instinct is the target.
steps.instructions: Read the payment request.

steps.name: What the Request Is Counting On

highlighterTexts: Start with the address, not the name. The display name says David Chen; the domain is meridiananalytics.co, not .com. This is the only part of the message that is actually checkable.
Urgency you did not create. A same-day emergency payment is out of character for a CFO who plans a fortnight ahead - and urgency is what stops people checking.
The normal process is skipped. No purchase order, no approval chain. A request to go around a control is a bigger signal than the amount.
"I can't discuss this now." The one instruction that matters: do not use another channel. Every line of this asks you not to verify, which is the reason to verify.

steps.description: Three questions answer almost every request like this: is it unusual, does it bypass a control, and does it discourage checking? All three are answerable from the message itself.
steps.instructions: Step through the request.

steps.name: Verify on a Channel He Does Not Control
steps.description: Replying would reach whoever owns that domain. Calling the extension in the company directory reaches David. Use the number you already have, never one the message supplies.
steps.instructions: Call David to verify.

steps.name: Report It
steps.description: David has confirmed it. He thinks his account may be compromised; security will establish whether that is true. Your job now is to get it on record.
steps.instructions: Open the incident portal and sign in.

steps.name: File the Report

variables.name: subject
variables.correctValue: BEC attack - fraudulent payment request impersonating David Chen

variables.name: description
variables.correctValue:
Received an email appearing to be from David Chen, sent from david.chen@meridiananalytics.co (a lookalike of our meridiananalytics.com domain), requesting an urgent $47,500 payment to an unknown vendor (TechStream Solutions). Red flags included: unusual urgency, bypassing normal approval process, sender being unavailable for discussion, and unrecognized vendor. Called David directly using his extension (Ext. 2150) to verify - he confirmed he did not send the email. No payment was processed.

The email has been preserved in my inbox for investigation.

steps.description: Include the sender address exactly as it appeared. It is the detail that lets security find the domain and file the abuse report.
steps.instructions: Complete and submit the incident report.

steps.name: What Security Actually Found

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Thank you for reporting this. The payment was never raised, so the $47,500 stayed where it was.

One correction worth passing on. David told us he thought his account had been compromised. It had not. Nothing of ours was broken into - the message came from meridiananalytics.co, a domain registered that morning for nine dollars. Every header was legitimate, because the sender genuinely owned the domain he was sending from. That is why none of our filters flagged it.

We have filed an abuse report with the registrar and asked them to suspend the domain.

The only control that worked here was you picking up the phone. There was nothing in the message itself to detect - just one character.

IT Security, Meridian Analytics
email.subject: Re: Incident Report - BEC Attack Prevented

steps.description: The response corrects an assumption worth correcting.
steps.instructions: Read the response from IT Security.

steps.name: Nothing Was Compromised

highlighterTexts: No account was compromised. The attacker owned the domain he sent from, so SPF, DKIM and every other header check passed honestly. The mail was not forged; it was simply from someone else.
That is why the filters were always going to let it through, and why 'our email security would have caught it' is not a plan.

steps.description: David assumed he had been hacked. Almost nobody had been.
steps.instructions: Review what security found.

steps.name: Nine Dollars, Gone

highlighterTexts: Suspended, and the mail routing withdrawn. The next person at Meridian to receive this exact attack will not receive it at all.
It cost him nine dollars and it cost Meridian nothing, because one person spent two minutes on a phone call instead of ninety seconds on a transfer.

steps.description: The abuse report lands with the registrar.
steps.instructions: See what the report cost him.

steps.name: The Audit Mindset
steps.description:
An audit mindset is not suspicion of people. It is refusing to let the shape of a request decide whether you check it.

Read the address, not the display name. The name is typed by the sender. The domain is the only part that has to be bought, and it is where lookalikes live.

Urgency is a request not to verify. Treat it as the signal rather than the reason. A legitimate request survives a two-minute delay.

Verify on a channel the sender does not control. Use the extension in the directory, not the number in the message; never reply to ask whether the message is real.

A skipped control is the loudest signal there is. Bigger than the amount, bigger than the tone.

Passing every technical check means nothing. Authenticated mail from a domain the attacker owns is still authenticated. The last control is a person.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

description: A request from a trusted name is exactly where a check is most likely to be skipped. Learn to pause before acting on a routine-looking request, spot the details that separate a real one from an impersonation, verify through contact details you already hold, and report an attempt even when nothing was lost.

actorDescriptions.bob: A threat actor who does not break into anything. He buys a domain that reads like his target's and writes a convincing email.
actorDescriptions.alice: You are Alice, an accounts payable analyst at Meridian Analytics. You have been here two years and you take pride in getting things right, which is exactly the instinct this request is built to use.

name: ISMS Policy Awareness

quiz.text: What is the practical consequence of a file never being entered in the asset register?

answers.text: It has no classification, so every downstream control treats it at the lowest tier
It cannot be sent outside the company at all
It is automatically treated as Confidential until reviewed
It is excluded from backups

quiz.text: A partner asks for a package containing client contract values and internal network detail. What does a Confidential label actually change about how it is sent?

answers.text: The gateway requires named recipients and an expiry date rather than a link anyone can open
The files are compressed before sending
The recipient receives a warning banner they must dismiss
Nothing changes about transmission; the label is for archiving

quiz.text: Why is a shared service account that is exempt from multi-factor prompts treated as a standing risk rather than a convenience?

answers.text: It belongs to no individual, so its misuse looks normal and nobody notices the credential has spread
Shared accounts are slower to authenticate
It cannot be given permissions at all
Auditors require every account to have a photograph on file

quiz.text: You have just realised a file you sent last week contained more than it should have. Nothing has obviously gone wrong yet. What does the ISMS expect of you?

answers.text: Report it straight away, before taking remedial action, so responders know what was exposed and the evidence is intact
Delete your copy and wait to see whether anything happens
Revoke everything you can first and report only if the revocation fails
Raise it at the next quarterly review so it can be discussed properly

quiz.text: Once a credential has been published in a file that left the company, what is the only effective remedy?

answers.text: Disable or rotate the account, and terminate any session already using it
Revoke the file's share link, which makes the credential unusable
Ask the recipient to delete their copy and confirm in writing
Reclassify the file as Confidential so the credential is covered retroactively

steps.name: The Handover Is Due

email.message:
Alice,

Solvane Operations take over Halberd monitoring on Monday, so they need the handover pack before the weekend. It is the design pack, the client roster and the monitoring notes.

Their handover mailbox is handover@solvaneops.co. Send it through SecureTransfer rather than email - the files are too big for a mail attachment anyway.

Open SecureTransfer

Thanks,
Priya
Programme Manager, Quantum Dynamics
email.subject: Halberd handover pack - please send today

highlighterTexts: The pack holds the design pack, the client roster and the monitoring notes, all going outside the company to a supplier.
Priya says to use SecureTransfer, the approved channel. How the pack is classified still decides who may receive it and for how long.

steps.description: Quantum Dynamics is handing monitoring of the Halberd programme over to a supplier, Solvane Operations. The programme manager wants the handover pack sent today. Read the request.
steps.instructions: Read the request from the programme manager.

steps.name: Open SecureTransfer
steps.description: SecureTransfer is the approved way to send large files outside Quantum Dynamics. Open it from the link in Priya's mail.
steps.instructions: Open SecureTransfer from the link in the email, look it over, then click Next.

steps.name: What the Gateway Knows About This Package

highlighterTexts: Unclassified. Not because anyone judged these files harmless, but because nobody ever recorded a judgement at all.
The label comes from the asset register, and this pack was never put in it. No entry means no label, and no label means the gateway treats the package at its lowest tier.
This is the whole mechanism. An ISMS decides how information is handled by what is written down about it, so information nobody wrote down gets handled as if it did not matter.

steps.description: Before you fill anything in, look at what SecureTransfer already believes about these files.
steps.instructions: Review what the gateway already knows about this package.

steps.name: Release the Package
steps.description: Address the package to Solvane's handover mailbox and release it. This is exactly what the job asks for, and nothing on this screen will stop you.
steps.instructions: Address the package to the supplier and release it.

steps.name: Released as Public

highlighterTexts: Released as Public. An unlabelled package falls to the bottom tier, so the gateway applied no controls at all.
Anyone with the link can open it. There is no sign-in, so there is no account to disable and no record of who collected the files.
It never expires. Whatever happens to that URL from now on, it keeps working.

steps.description: The package is on its way. Read the three lines the gateway printed underneath the link, because they describe something much larger than one email.
steps.instructions: Read the release terms the gateway printed.

steps.name: Who Decided That?

answers.text: The pack was never entered in the asset register, so it carried no classification for the gateway to act on
answers.explanation: Classification is the input every downstream control reads. With no register entry there is no label, and with no label the gateway has nothing to enforce.

answers.text: Alice chose the wrong sharing setting on the release form
answers.explanation: There was no sharing setting to choose. That is the point - the decision had already been made somewhere she never saw.

answers.text: SecureTransfer was misconfigured and should default to Confidential
answers.explanation: Defaulting everything to Confidential sounds safer but makes the label meaningless, so people work around it. The gateway behaved exactly as designed; the register was the gap.

answers.text: The supplier's mailbox was not approved for external transfers
answers.explanation: Solvane were a legitimate, contracted supplier and the right recipient. Nothing about the destination was wrong.

data.question: Alice filled the form in correctly and broke no rule on the screen. What made the package public?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: A Mailbox Nobody Watches
steps.description: Solvane Operations is a twelve-person supplier. Their shared handover mailbox has one password, no second factor, and four people who have left still know it. Bob bought that password three weeks ago and has been reading the mailbox ever since.
steps.instructions: Watch what the attacker finds in the supplier mailbox, then click Next.

steps.name: No Sign-In, No Expiry

highlighterTexts: Sign-in required: No. The page never asks who he is, so nothing he does here appears in anyone's access log under a name.
Recipient restriction: None. The link was addressed to Solvane, but it was never bound to them. Forwarded, pasted, or stolen, it works the same.
Expires: Never. If he does nothing today he can come back in a year and it will still be here.

steps.description: He did not need Solvane's password to open this. He only needed the link that was sitting in their inbox.
steps.instructions: Review the terms the link was published under.

steps.name: Take the Package
steps.description: Watch him collect the files. No credential is spent, and no alert fires.
steps.instructions: Download the package.

steps.name: What Was Inside

highlighterTexts: The monitoring notes name the gateway, the internal address range, and a shared service account with its secret written beside it.

Shared, and exempt from multi-factor prompts. That exemption exists because a rota cannot answer a push notification at three in the morning - and it is exactly what makes the account usable by anyone holding the string.
None of this was left in the package on purpose. It was in a file that nobody had ever classified, so nobody had ever been required to strip it.

steps.description: The client roster alone is worth money. The third file is worth considerably more.
steps.instructions: Look at what the handover notes contain.

steps.name: Sign In With the Handover Account
steps.description: He does not need to break anything. He types in what the file gave him.
steps.instructions: Sign in with the account from the handover notes.

steps.name: Open the Tunnel
steps.description: The gateway accepted the account without a second factor, exactly as the notes said it would.
steps.instructions: Open the tunnel.

steps.name: Inside the Network

highlighterTexts: He is no longer looking at one handover pack. He is on the inside of the network, reachable to the file shares, the contract database and the personnel records.
The backup store matters most. It holds copies of everything the other three hosts have ever contained, which is why it is usually the first thing taken.
Every packet he sends is attributed to svc-monitor - an account that belongs to a rota rather than a person, so no individual's absence makes the session look odd.

steps.description: This is what one unclassified file bought him.
steps.instructions: Review what the tunnel reaches.

steps.name: The Shape of the Exposure

answers.text: The asset was unregistered, so it went out unclassified; unclassified meant a public link; the public link carried a shared credential that opened the network
answers.explanation: Each control depends on the one before it. Asset management feeds classification, classification feeds transfer handling, and the contents of what is transferred feed identity. Missing the first one removed all three.

answers.text: The supplier's mailbox was compromised, so everything after it was unavoidable
answers.explanation: The compromised mailbox is the trigger, not the cause. A package bound to named recipients, with an expiry and no credential inside it, survives a compromised mailbox with very little damage.

answers.text: The service account had no multi-factor authentication, which is the root cause
answers.explanation: That exemption made the last step easy, but the credential should never have been in a file leaving the company. Fixing only the account leaves the leak intact.

answers.text: Alice sent the pack to the wrong address
answers.explanation: She sent it to the correct supplier, at the address the programme manager gave her. Nothing about her action was a mistake in itself.

data.question: Three separate ISMS controls failed in sequence here. Which ordering describes what actually happened?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: The SOC Calls It In

email.message:
Alice,

We have an open tunnel on gw-04 authenticated as svc-monitor from a network that has never appeared in our logs, at a time when nobody on the rota was working.

Tracing backwards, the account secret appears in network-handover.txt, which went out two days ago inside SecureTransfer package QD-7841. That package was released unclassified, which means it went out as a public link with no recipient restriction and no expiry. It has been downloaded once by someone who is not Solvane.

You released the package, so the corrective actions are yours to complete. Please:
  • file the incident so the ticket has a record from your side
  • register and classify the asset
  • revoke the released link
  • disable the shared account

Open the ISMS portal

Security Operations, Quantum Dynamics
email.subject: QD-INC-2291 - svc-monitor tunnel from an unrecognised network

highlighterTexts: A svc-monitor secret inside network-handover.txt let someone open a tunnel on gw-04 from an unknown network.
The package went out unclassified, so it became a public link with no recipient restriction and no expiry.
The fix is in your hands: file the incident, register and classify the asset, revoke the link and disable the shared account.

steps.description: Two days later the security operations team notices a tunnel that does not fit the on-call rota. Read what they found.
steps.instructions: Read the alert from Security Operations.

steps.name: Sign In to the ISMS Portal
steps.description: Everything the SOC asked for lives in the ISMS portal. Open it and sign in.
steps.instructions: Open the ISMS portal and sign in.

steps.name: File the Incident

variables.name: description
variables.correctValue: I released the Halberd handover pack to handover@solvaneops.co through SecureTransfer two days ago. The pack was not in the asset register, so it went out unclassified and the gateway published it as a public link with no recipient restriction and no expiry. One of the files, network-handover.txt, contained the gateway address, the internal address range and the secret for the shared svc-monitor account. The link has been downloaded once by someone other than Solvane, and a tunnel has since been opened with that account.

variables.name: actions-taken
variables.correctValue: None yet. Reporting first so the ticket has a record of what was in the package before I start revoking anything.

steps.description: Report it from your side. The SOC saw the tunnel; only you can say what left and when. Fill the report in and submit it.
steps.instructions: Open the incident report and file it.

steps.name: Why That Report Earns Its Place

highlighterTexts: The package reference turns a vague exposure into one object they can pull the full download log for.
You named the file that carried the credential. The SOC found the tunnel; only you knew what else was in the package.
That is why the reporter's account is not redundant with the alert. Detection tells you something is happening; the reporter tells you what is at stake.
Saying you have done nothing yet is useful, not embarrassing. It tells the responders the evidence is still intact and nothing has been overwritten.

steps.description: Incident management is one of the ISMS domains that only works if ordinary people use it. Look at what your report gave the responders.
steps.instructions: Review what your report gave the responders.

steps.name: The Corrective Actions
steps.description: The ticket lists three fixes, one for each control that failed. Open the corrective actions page.
steps.instructions: Open the corrective actions page.

steps.name: Register and Label the Asset
steps.description: Start where the failure started. The pack holds client identities, contract values and internal network detail. Read the label definitions on the card, choose the label those contents call for, and register the asset.
steps.instructions: Choose the right classification and register the asset.

steps.name: Revoke the Released Link
steps.description: The label fixes the next release. It does nothing about the copy already in circulation. Withdraw package QD-7841.
steps.instructions: Revoke package QD-7841.

steps.name: Disable the Shared Account
steps.description: The secret is out and cannot be called back, so the account it unlocks has to stop existing. Disable svc-monitor.
steps.instructions: Disable the svc-monitor account.

steps.name: He Goes Back for the Link

highlighterTexts: Withdrawn. The link had no expiry, so the only thing that could ever stop it was somebody deciding to.

steps.description: He kept the URL. It cost him nothing to keep, and until yesterday it worked.
steps.instructions: Watch the attacker return to the link, look the page over, then click Next.

steps.name: He Still Has the Secret
steps.description: The credential in his notes has not changed a character. Watch him use it.
steps.instructions: Watch the attacker reuse the stolen secret.

steps.name: Refused

highlighterTexts: The secret is still correct. It is the account that is gone, which is the only remedy available once a credential has left the building.
The tunnel he already had was cut too. Disabling an account that is in use has to kill the live session as well, or the attacker simply keeps the one he has.

steps.description: Same account, same secret, different answer.
steps.instructions: Read what the gateway answers this time.

steps.name: Closing the Ticket

email.message:
Alice,

The tunnel is dead, the link is withdrawn and the pack is registered as Confidential. Thank you for reporting it from your side; the SOC had the session but not the contents, and your report is what told them a credential was in play.

For the record, this is what the ISMS is for. Four of its domains touched this one incident:
  • Asset management - the pack was not in the register, so nothing downstream knew it existed
  • Classification - with no label, the transfer gateway had no rule to apply
  • Identity management - a shared account exempt from multi-factor turned a document leak into network access
  • Incident management - reporting it quickly is what made the other three fixable in a day rather than a quarter

Two changes go in this week. SecureTransfer will refuse to release anything that is not in the asset register, and the on-call rota moves off shared accounts onto named ones.

Tomas Aldridge
ISMS Manager, Quantum Dynamics
email.subject: QD-INC-2291 closed - and what changes

highlighterTexts: Four ISMS domains touched this one incident: asset management, classification, identity management and incident management.
Alice's report told the SOC a credential was in play, which is why the other fixes took a day rather than a quarter.

steps.description: The ISMS manager closes QD-INC-2291 and records what changes because of it.
steps.instructions: Read the closing note from the ISMS manager.

steps.name: What the ISMS Actually Did
steps.description:
An ISMS is not a binder you read once a year. It is a chain of controls that each read the one before them.

An unregistered asset has no classification. Every handling rule downstream - who may receive it, whether it expires, whether it may leave at all - is decided by a label, and a label only exists if somebody registered the thing.

Credentials do not belong in deliverables. The handover notes were written to be helpful. Classification is what would have forced somebody to strip the secret before it left.

Shared accounts turn one leak into many. An account with no owner cannot be missed, cannot answer a multi-factor prompt, and cannot be traced to a person.

Reporting is a control, not a courtesy. Detection saw a strange tunnel. Only the person who sent the package knew what was inside it, and that is what made the rest fixable the same day.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

description: An information security management system ties asset registration, classification, access control and incident reporting into one set of controls. Learn how an unregistered, unclassified file escapes the rules meant to protect it, then report the exposure, classify and register the asset, and contain the leak.

name: Internet & Email Acceptable Use

quiz.text: Which activities are PROHIBITED on company networks? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Checking cryptocurrency platforms during lunch
Briefly checking personal email during a break
Streaming Netflix during lunch
Downloading software from unvetted websites
Reading news articles during a break

quiz.text: Why should confidential documents never be sent to personal email?

answers.text: It's against policy but not actually dangerous
Personal email lacks enterprise security controls
It uses too much bandwidth
It's fine if you delete the email afterward

quiz.text: What should you do if a colleague asks to use your computer for a prohibited activity?

answers.text: Allow it since it's their responsibility, not yours
Politely decline and explain that the activity is prohibited
Let them use it but report it afterward
Log out so they can use their own credentials

quiz.text: What was a mitigating factor in Alice's case that reduced the severity of consequences?

answers.text: She didn't actually access any confidential data
The report never reached her personal email
She filed a full, honest self-report and cooperated
Her manager vouched for her work ethic

quiz.text: A friend recommends a financial analysis tool from an unfamiliar website. What should you do?

answers.text: Download it if the site looks professional
Check with IT Security whether the site and tool are permitted
Use it only during lunch breaks
Download it to a USB drive first to be safe

steps.name: Late Night at Northgate Financial
steps.description: It's 7 PM on a Wednesday — you're working late to finish the Q3 Client Portfolio Analysis, due first thing tomorrow morning. The office is mostly empty.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: A Helpful Tip

telegramMessage.text: Hey Alice! Working late on market analysis? Check out CryptoPulse — cryptopulse.io. They have a free Market Insight Toolkit that's amazing for financial trend visualization. Way better than what most firms provide. I use it for everything now.

highlighterTexts: Jake is recommending an unvetted external tool from a website Alice hasn't verified with IT. Even well-meaning recommendations can lead to prohibited sites or malware.

steps.description: Alice's phone buzzes. It's a message from Jake Torres — a friend and former colleague who now works at a hedge fund.
steps.instructions: Read the message from Jake.

steps.name: Visiting CryptoPulse
steps.note: Many prohibited sites look professional and legitimate. The policy exists because these sites often contain malvertising, tracking scripts, and create conflict-of-interest risks in financial services.
steps.description:
Alice opens CryptoPulse in her work browser. The site looks professional — market charts, analysis tools, portfolio tracking. It doesn't look like a shady crypto site at all.

But Northgate's acceptable use policy explicitly prohibits cryptocurrency platforms on company networks, regardless of how professional they appear.
steps.instructions: Open the CryptoPulse website.

steps.name: The Free Toolkit

highlighterTexts: The "Free Market Insight Toolkit" banner catches Alice's eye. Downloading software from unvetted sources is a security risk — and this site is prohibited on company networks.

steps.description: A banner on the site offers a "Free Market Insight Toolkit." Alice thinks it could help with her analysis. She clicks download without thinking twice.
steps.instructions: Notice the download banner and download the toolkit.

steps.name: The Download Warning
steps.note: Never dismiss antivirus warnings. Security software is your last line of defense — if it flags a file as suspicious, stop and verify with IT.

data.name: MarketInsight_Toolkit_v2.1.exe
data.text:
Threat Detected: Adware.CryptoPulse.Tracker

The file 'MarketInsight_Toolkit_v2.1.exe' has been flagged as potentially unwanted software. This file is designed to:
- Install browser tracking components
- Modify browser settings
- Collect browsing activity data

Recommendation: Do not run this file. Report to IT Security.

steps.description: The company's endpoint protection flags the download. A warning pops up — but Alice is in a rush and dismisses it. "It's just a false positive," she thinks. "Jake uses this tool every day."
steps.instructions: Dismiss the antivirus warning.

steps.name: The Shortcut Home
steps.note: Company data classified as Confidential must never be sent to personal email addresses. Personal email lacks enterprise security controls.

email.message:
Hi me,

Attaching the Q3 Client Portfolio Analysis to finish at home tonight. Will delete after.

— Alice
email.subject: Q3 report draft — finish at home

steps.description:
It's getting late. Alice decides to email the Q3 report draft to her personal email to finish at home. She sends the confidential Q3_Client_Portfolio_Analysis.xlsx to alice.morgan.personal@gmail.com.

"It's faster than the secure file transfer," she tells herself. The report contains confidential client portfolio values, investment strategies, and personal financial details.

steps.name: A Productive Evening

The site also installed a tracking cookie on your machine.
The downloaded file (MarketInsight_Toolkit_v2.1.exe) was quarantined by endpoint protection.

The confidential Q3 Client Portfolio Analysis was forwarded to a personal Gmail address.

answers.text: The company doesn't want employees distracted

answers.text: Conflict-of-interest concerns, regulatory requirements, and security risks from malvertising
answers.explanation: Financial firms face strict SEC/FINRA regulations. Crypto platforms create conflict-of-interest risks, and many contain malvertising that can compromise corporate networks.

answers.text: Cryptocurrency is illegal
answers.explanation: Cryptocurrency is legal but restricted on company systems due to regulatory and security concerns specific to financial services.

Alice,

email.subject: Outcome: Policy Violation Review — Alice Morgan

highlighterTexts: Alice's full, honest self-report was noted as a mitigating factor. The consequences — a written warning, 90-day monitoring, and retraining — are serious but manageable. Honesty and full cooperation kept the outcome manageable.

telegramMessage.text: Hey Alice! My personal laptop is in the shop and I want to check my crypto portfolio during lunch. Can I use your computer for a few minutes? I'll just log into my Coinbase account real quick.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description: Congratulations on completing the Internet & Email Acceptable Use training. Company networks are for business purposes. Limited personal use during breaks is fine, but prohibited categories (crypto, gambling, streaming, unauthorized software) are never permitted — even if sites look professional. Never forward confidential data to personal email. Personal accounts lack enterprise security controls. Use approved secure transfer tools instead. Don't download software from unvetted sources. Even if a colleague recommends it. Endpoint protection may catch it, but the risk isn't worth it. Web filtering, endpoint protection and DLP log this activity. Sites visited, email attachments, downloads — it's all monitored. This isn't about surveillance, it's about protecting client data and meeting regulatory requirements. Self-reporting matters. Being honest about mistakes demonstrates integrity and typically results in less severe consequences. Politely decline prohibited requests from colleagues. Lending your workstation for prohibited activities makes YOU accountable.

name: Employee Security Responsibilities

quiz.text: A caller claims to be from IT and says your account has been compromised. They ask you to verify your identity by providing your password. What should you do?

answers.text: Provide your password since they're trying to help protect your account
Hang up and contact IT directly through the company directory to verify the claim
Ask the caller to prove they're from IT by telling you your employee ID
Give them a fake password to test if they're legitimate

quiz.text: Why was the caller's offer to "verify" himself a trick?

answers.text: He gave part of his employee ID and got the victim to read out the rest, so the proof came from the victim
Because employee IDs can never be used to verify anyone
Because only IT is allowed to look up employee IDs
It was not a trick; confirming part of an ID is a reliable check

quiz.text: The phishing page in this exercise used the domain meridianhc-portal.net. What made this a red flag?

answers.text: The page loaded slowly
It was not the official meridianhc.com domain: attackers registered a similar-looking domain
It used HTTPS instead of HTTP
The page had a different color scheme

quiz.text: Why do social engineers use urgency (like a "dying patient") in their attacks?

answers.text: Because real emergencies happen frequently in healthcare
To make the victim act before they have time to think critically or verify the request
Because urgent situations require bypassing security protocols
To make the call seem more believable to IT monitoring systems

quiz.text: After realizing she fell for a social engineering attack, what is the MOST important thing Alice should do?

answers.text: Delete the phishing page from her browser history
Wait to see if anything actually happens before reporting
Report the incident immediately and change her compromised credentials
Try to log into the phishing site again to confirm it was fake

quiz.text: Which of the following are reliable ways to verify a caller's identity? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Check the caller ID displayed on your phone
Hang up and call the person's department using the official company directory
Ask the caller to read you their employee ID
Walk to the person's office or department to verify in person

steps.name: A Normal Monday at Meridian Healthcare
steps.description: It's a normal Monday morning. You've just settled in with your coffee and logged into the patient management portal.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: An Urgent Phone Call
steps.note: The caller's urgency is designed to bypass your critical thinking. Real emergencies have established protocols, and they never require sharing credentials over the phone.
steps.description: Alice's phone rings. The caller ID shows "Dr. Rajan Mehta - Cardiology." The man on the line sounds urgent, almost panicked, and needs help getting into patient records.
steps.instructions: Answer the incoming phone call.

steps.name: The Verification Trick
steps.note: This is a fake verification. The caller offers part of a detail and gets the victim to supply the rest, so the "proof" comes from the victim, not from the caller. Real verification runs the other way: you check what the caller tells you against a source you already trust.
steps.description: The caller offers to "verify" his identity. He gives Alice the first few digits of his employee ID and asks her to look up and read back the rest. It feels like proof, but he just tricked Alice into completing his identity for him.
steps.instructions: Listen to the caller's verification request.

steps.name: Directed to the "Quick-Reset Tool"
steps.description: Now that Alice believes the caller is legitimate, he sends her to an "IT quick-reset tool" and asks her to authorize the reset with her own credentials.
steps.instructions: Listen as the caller provides the URL.

steps.name: Entering Credentials on the Phishing Page
steps.description: Alice opens the URL the caller provided. The page looks like a Meridian Healthcare IT tool, but the domain is meridianhc-portal.net, not the real meridianhc.com. She doesn't notice the difference in her rush to help the "dying patient."
steps.instructions: Open the browser and navigate to the URL the caller provided. Enter your credentials to "authorize" the reset.

steps.name: "Processing" the Authorization
steps.description: The page shows a "Processing Authorization" message and says Alice will receive a confirmation email within 24 hours. It looks routine, but her credentials have just been captured by the attacker.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Consequences Revealed

email.message:
Alice,

We have detected unauthorized access to the Meridian Healthcare patient management system using your credentials.

Scope of breach:
  • 2,300 patient records accessed and exported
  • Data includes names, DOBs, SSNs, insurance IDs, and medical history
  • Access originated from an external IP address
Your access to the patient management system has been suspended pending investigation. Log in to the security portal with your current password to review the incident, then change it. A full HIPAA breach investigation has been launched.

Please review the incident report at security.meridianhc.com/breach-report immediately.

Diana Torres, CISO
email.subject: URGENT: Security Breach: Your Credentials Compromised

highlighterTexts: The credentials Alice typed into the fake reset tool were used to export 2,300 patient records to an external IP address.
This is a genuine email from the meridianhc.com domain. Her access is suspended and a HIPAA breach investigation has started.

steps.description:
Three hours later, an urgent email arrives from the CISO. Unauthorized access has been detected on the patient management system. 2,300 patient records, with names, Social Security numbers, insurance data and medical histories, have been exported to an external server.

The credentials used: Alice's.
steps.instructions: Read the urgent email from the CISO.

steps.name: The Breach Investigation
steps.description: Alice's stomach drops. She clicks the link to the breach investigation dashboard and logs in to see the full scope of the damage.
steps.instructions: Click the incident report link and log in to the security portal.

steps.name: Understanding the Attack Chain

highlighterTexts: Red Flag #1: The caller was never verified through official channels. Alice accepted a spoofed caller ID and a partial employee ID as proof, but the attacker supplied the partial ID and had Alice fill in the rest.
Red Flag #2: The URL was meridianhc-portal.net, not the real meridianhc.com domain that every Meridian tool uses. The phishing page sat on an external domain the attacker controlled.
The damage: 2,300 patient records stolen. HIPAA breach notification required within 60 days. Estimated regulatory exposure: $500K+. All from one phone call and one form submission.

steps.description: The breach dashboard reveals the full attack chain. Every step is laid out: the spoofed caller ID, the fake verification trick, the phishing URL on an external domain, and the credential capture.
steps.instructions: Review the highlighted entries in the timeline showing the attack chain.

steps.name: What Should Alice Have Done?

answers.text: Help the doctor immediately: a patient's life is at stake
answers.explanation: Urgency is the #1 social engineering tactic. Real medical emergencies have established protocols that never require sharing credentials over the phone. The attacker weaponized Alice's compassion.

answers.text: Hang up and call the Cardiology department directly using the official directory to verify
answers.explanation: Always verify callers independently through official channels. Look up the number yourself. Never use a number the caller provides. If it's a real emergency, the doctor will understand the 2-minute verification.

answers.text: Ask the caller more questions to determine if they're real
answers.explanation: Social engineers are experts at answering questions convincingly. The only reliable verification is contacting the person through a completely separate, known-good channel, like calling their department directly.

answers.text: Check the caller ID to confirm it's an internal number
answers.explanation: Caller ID can be easily spoofed. The attacker made the call appear to come from an internal extension. Caller ID is NOT a reliable form of identity verification.

data.question: When the caller claimed to be a doctor needing an urgent password reset, what should Alice have done?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: Remediation: Change Compromised Password
steps.description: As the first remediation step, Alice must immediately change her compromised password. Her old credentials are in the hands of the attacker.
steps.instructions: Navigate to Account Settings and change your password.

steps.name: Remediation: Set Up Multi-Factor Authentication

highlighterTexts: This is why MFA matters. Even if an attacker steals your password through phishing, the password alone is no longer enough to log in. One stolen credential should never be enough to breach an account.

steps.description: With the password changed, there's one more critical step. If MFA had been enabled, the attacker's stolen password alone would not have been enough to access Alice's account. MFA requires a second verification - like a code from an authenticator app - that the attacker doesn't have.
steps.instructions: Click "Set Up" to begin enabling MFA on your account.

steps.name: Authenticator Setup

highlighterTexts: The authenticator app generates a new 6-digit code every 30 seconds. Even if an attacker has your password, they would also need this code. Never read it out or type it in because a caller asked.

steps.description: The security portal now displays a QR code. Alice needs to scan this with her phone's authenticator app. The app will generate a unique verification code that changes every 30 seconds - this is the second factor that means a stolen password alone is not enough.
steps.instructions: Review the setup instructions, then open your phone to scan the QR code.

steps.name: Scan the QR Code
steps.description: The portal displays a QR code for setting up the authenticator. Alice needs to open the authenticator app on her phone and scan the code.
steps.instructions: Open the Authenticator app on your phone and scan the QR code.

steps.name: Copy the Verification Code
steps.description: The authenticator app has generated a 6-digit verification code. Alice needs to copy it and enter it on the security portal to complete MFA setup.
steps.instructions: Copy the verification code from the authenticator app.

steps.name: Verify and Enable MFA
steps.description: Alice enters the verification code on the security portal to confirm her authenticator is working correctly.
steps.instructions: Enter the verification code and submit to enable MFA.

steps.name: Remediation: File Incident Report

variables.name: description
variables.correctValue:
Received a phone call from someone claiming to be Dr. Rajan Mehta from Cardiology. Caller ID showed internal extension.

Caller claimed a patient was coding and needed an urgent portal password reset. He provided a partial employee ID (EMP-78) and I verified the rest. He directed me to meridianhc-portal.net/reset where I entered my credentials to authorize the reset.

The URL was NOT the real meridianhc.com domain. Three hours later, 2,300 patient records were accessed using my compromised credentials.

steps.description: Next, Alice must file a formal incident report documenting the social engineering attack. This report will be critical for the HIPAA breach investigation and helps the security team warn other employees.
steps.instructions: Navigate to the incident report form and submit a detailed description of the attack.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description: Congratulations on completing this training. Verify callers independently, always. If someone calls claiming urgency, hang up and call their department through the official directory. Never trust caller ID alone. It can be spoofed. If it's a real emergency, they'll understand the verification. Never enter credentials on unfamiliar URLs. Check the domain carefully before typing any password. The real Meridian portal is meridianhc.com, and the phishing page was meridianhc-portal.net. One added word and a different ending (.net) were the difference between safety and a 2,300-record breach. Urgency is a weapon. Social engineers create artificial time pressure to bypass your critical thinking. "A patient is dying" or "your account will be locked" are designed to make you act before you think. Slow down. Enable MFA: passwords alone are not enough. If Alice had MFA enabled, her stolen password alone would not have been enough for the attacker. Never read out or type in a code because a caller asked for it. Multi-factor authentication is one of the most effective defenses against credential theft. Report everything, even if you made a mistake. Alice's incident report helped the security team contain the breach faster. Reporting is not about blame, it's about damage control. The worst thing you can do is stay silent.
steps.instructions: Click Next to proceed to the quiz.

description: Social engineers use urgency, authority and appeals to compassion to get credentials out of whoever answers. Learn to verify an unexpected caller through the internal directory, spot a lookalike portal, contain a compromised account, and report what the caller claimed.

name: Audit Portal Training

quiz.text: What is the primary purpose of a Security Audit Portal?

answers.text: To monitor employee productivity and internet usage
To centralize security reporting, tracking, and maintain compliance audit trails
To automatically block all suspicious emails
To replace the IT help desk for technical support

quiz.text: Which of the following are best practices when submitting a security report? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Report early rather than waiting to investigate yourself
Include specific details like dates, times, and sender information
Delete suspicious emails after reporting to clean your inbox
Preserve evidence for the investigation team
Wait until you're certain it's a real threat before reporting

quiz.text: Why is accurate report categorization important?

answers.text: It determines how much your annual bonus will be
It ensures the report is routed to the appropriate team for faster response
It prevents the report from being logged permanently
It allows you to bypass management approval

quiz.text: What requirements make Security Audit Portals important in financial services?

answers.text: There are no regulatory requirements - it's just a convenience
Rules and standards such as the GLBA Safeguards Rule and PCI DSS require a documented incident response process
Only physical security incidents need to be documented
Regulations only apply to banks, not other financial services

quiz.text: What happens to reports submitted through the Audit Portal?

answers.text: They are automatically deleted after 30 days
They become part of a tamper-evident audit trail kept for the required retention period
They are only visible to the person who submitted them
They are forwarded to external regulators immediately

quiz.text: Which red flags should prompt you to report an email through the Audit Portal? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Urgent requests for payment information changes
Sender domain that doesn't match the claimed organization
A routine meeting invitation from your manager
Generic greetings and lack of specific context
Requests that bypass normal verification procedures

steps.name: Welcome to Apex Financial
steps.description: Today, you'll learn how to use the company's Security Audit Portal - a centralized system for reporting security concerns, tracking incidents, and ensuring regulatory compliance.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Why Audit Portals Matter
steps.note: Regulatory bodies require financial institutions to maintain detailed records of security incidents. A centralized portal makes compliance audits much smoother.
steps.description:
In financial services, security incidents must be documented properly. The GLBA Safeguards Rule and the PCI DSS card-industry standard both require a documented incident response process. The Security Audit Portal ensures:
  • All security concerns are logged and tracked
  • Incidents are routed to the right team automatically
  • You can monitor the status of your reports
  • The company maintains an audit trail for regulators
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: A Suspicious Email Arrives

email.message:
Dear Apex Financial Team,

We have updated our banking details for all future payments. Please update your records immediately to avoid service interruption.

New Bank Details:
Bank: First National Trust
Account: 8827364501
Routing: 021000089

Please confirm receipt of this information.

Best regards,
Accounts Department
email.subject: URGENT: Updated Banking Information Required

steps.description:
Alice receives an email that doesn't feel right. It claims to be from a vendor requesting updated payment information, but something seems off about the formatting and urgency.

Rather than ignore it or try to investigate alone, Alice decides to report it through the proper channel.
steps.instructions: Open your email inbox and read the suspicious message.

steps.name: Identifying Red Flags

highlighterTexts: The sender domain 'vendor-payments-update.net' is not a recognized vendor domain.
Legitimate vendors use their official company domains for payment communications.
Generic greeting ('Dear Apex Financial Team') instead of addressing a specific person.
Urgency without context - no explanation of WHY banking details changed.
No reference to existing contract numbers or prior communications.

steps.description: Before reporting, Alice takes a moment to identify what specifically makes this email suspicious. This information will help the security team investigate.
steps.instructions: Review the highlighted concerns about this email.

steps.name: Accessing the Audit Portal
steps.description: Now Alice will access the Security Audit Portal to submit a report. The portal is available at audit.apexfinancial.com and requires authentication for security purposes.
steps.instructions: Log in to the Security Audit Portal.

steps.name: Understanding the Dashboard
steps.description:
The Audit Portal dashboard shows several key sections:
  • New Report - Submit a new security concern
  • My Reports - Track reports you've submitted
  • Knowledge Base - Learn about security threats
  • Emergency Contacts - Direct lines to security team
Alice clicks 'New Report' to begin documenting the suspicious email.
steps.instructions: Click the 'New Report' button to start a security report.

steps.name: Selecting Report Type
steps.note: Accurate categorization speeds up response times. Security teams prioritize and route reports based on type.
steps.description:
The portal offers several report categories. Choosing the right type ensures your report is routed to the appropriate team.
  • Phishing / Social Engineering - Suspicious emails, calls, or messages
  • Data Breach / Exposure - Potential unauthorized data access
  • Policy Violation - Internal policy concerns
  • Physical Security - Unauthorized access, tailgating
  • Other - Anything that doesn't fit above
steps.instructions: Select 'Phishing / Social Engineering' as the report type.

steps.name: Completing the Report Form

variables.name: description
variables.correctValue:
Received an email from 'accounts@vendor-payments-update.net' requesting updated banking information.

Red flags: unknown sender domain, generic greeting, urgency without context, no reference to existing contracts. No links were clicked and no information was provided. Email is preserved in inbox for investigation.

steps.description:
Alice fills out the report with specific, factual details. Good reports include:
  • What happened (received suspicious email)
  • When it occurred (today's date/time)
  • Who was involved (sender details)
  • Why it's suspicious (red flags identified)
  • What action was taken (no links clicked, reporting now)
steps.instructions: Complete the incident description and submit the report.

steps.name: Report Submitted Successfully
steps.description:
The portal confirms Alice's report has been submitted. She receives a ticket number (SEC-2024-0847) for tracking.

The report is now in the security team's queue for review. Most reports are triaged within 4 hours during business days.
steps.instructions: Click 'View My Reports' to see the report status.

steps.name: Tracking Your Reports
steps.description:
The 'My Reports' section shows all reports Alice has submitted. Each entry displays:
  • Ticket ID - Unique reference number
  • Subject - What the report is about
  • Type - Report category
  • Status - New, In Progress, Resolved
  • Date - When it was submitted
steps.instructions: Click on the ticket to view details.

steps.name: Understanding the Workflow
steps.note: The audit trail is tamper-evident and kept for the required retention period. This supports regulatory compliance and accountability.
steps.description: The ticket details show the audit trail, a record of each milestone that sits alongside the overall status shown in the list: 1. Report Created - Your initial report 2. Pending Assignment - Waiting for a security analyst to take ownership 3. Investigation - Team reviews and investigates 4. Resolution - Actions taken, findings documented You can add comments if you discover additional information.
steps.instructions: Click Next to see the security team's response.

steps.name: Security Team Response

email.message:
Hi Alice, Thank you for reporting the suspicious vendor email (Ticket SEC-2024-0847). Investigation Findings: The email was confirmed as a Business Email Compromise (BEC) attempt. The domain 'vendor-payments-update.net' was registered 3 days ago and has been used in similar attacks against other financial institutions. Actions Taken:
  • Domain blocked at email gateway
  • Alert sent to Accounts Payable team
  • Vendor contact list verified - no legitimate vendors use this domain
  • Incident logged for regulatory reporting
Your Impact: Your quick reporting prevented a potential fraud attempt. Had this been actioned, it could have resulted in misdirected payments. Ticket Status: Resolved Thank you for your vigilance! Security Operations Center Apex Financial Services
email.subject: RE: SEC-2024-0847 - Investigation Complete

highlighterTexts: The email Alice reported was a confirmed Business Email Compromise attempt from a domain registered only three days earlier.
Because she reported it, the domain was blocked at the gateway and Accounts Payable was warned before any payment was misdirected.

steps.description: A few hours later, Alice receives an email from the Security Operations Center confirming they've investigated her report.
steps.instructions: Read the email from the Security Team.

steps.name: Best Practices for Reporting
steps.description:
Remember these best practices when using the Audit Portal:
  • Report early - Don't wait to investigate yourself
  • Be specific - Include dates, times, names, and screenshots if possible
  • Preserve evidence - Don't delete suspicious emails or files
  • Follow up - Check your ticket status and add information if needed
  • No retaliation - You're protected when reporting in good faith
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description:
Congratulations on completing the Audit Portal Training! Key lessons:
  • The Security Audit Portal is your first stop for any security concern
  • Accurate report categorization speeds up response times
  • Good reports are specific, factual, and timely
  • The portal creates an audit trail for regulatory compliance
  • You can track your reports and see investigation outcomes
  • Your reports directly contribute to organizational security

actorDescriptions.alice: You are Alice, a client services representative at Apex Financial Services. You handle customer accounts and financial transactions.
